newsitem.title: USA: Two Conn. towns pension bond sales still stalled.
newsitem.headline: Two Conn. towns pension bond sales still stalled.

text.p: Stratford and New Britain in Connecticut both came close to issuing taxable pension bonds, a step being considered by a few states and cities, but these two towns' plans remain stalled, officials said on Monday.

Ed Gomeau, director of finance for Stratford, which is located on the Long Island Sound about 20 miles south of New Haven, said that because the proposed $90 million taxable bond sale was not approved late last year by a super-majority of the town council, Stratford might have to come up with another $2 million in its fiscal 1998 budget.

"Raising the budget by $2 million would put substantial pressure on us so we're trying to work out some way of handling this," Gomeau said. The town, which has around 50,000 residents, had a budget of around $105 million in fiscal 1997.

The extra funds would be in addition to the $4.6 million already budgeted for the pension for next year. Stratford is facing a large unfunded pension liability--estimated at $660 million in 1993, a number that has grown since then.

Selling the taxable bonds would have saved Stratford from $40 million to $200 million, depending on which of various estimates is used, Gomeau said, adding that after the plan failed to get the votes it needed, "A majority of the council indicated they wished to keep the proposal alive."

The town's financial director that while the fiscal 1998 budget, which the town manager is due to propose in late March, is expected to resolve this issue, Stratford also must deal with a similar shortfall for the 1997 fiscal year. Changing the town ordinance that sets how much it must contribute to the plan is another possibility, he explained.

New Britain's plan to sell around $112 million of taxable bonds to cover an unfunded pension liability remains in limbo and it is continuing to stick with a funding plan devised by actuaries, according to John Jedrzejczyk, finance director.

He explained that the town officials were working on the budget, which in fiscal 1997 totaled about $140 million, and the issue might be addressed in that plan, which is expected to be adopted in June.
"People are working their way through the budget adoption. They might want to consider it," he said.

The town of 72,000, which is located about 10 miles southwest of Hartford in central Connecticut, would have saved about $15 million by selling the taxable bonds last September, when the plan was put forward, the town official added.
